A photon is the smallest possible, indivisible unit of light — and of all electromagnetic radiation. Think of it as a single, tiny packet of energy that travels through space. If you imagine light as a stream of water, a photon would be one individual molecule of water — the irreducible building block you cannot break down any further.

The word is used in physics to refer to this elementary particle. When physicists say a light bulb "emits photons," they mean it sends out a continuous stream of these tiny energy packets in all directions.
Light is both a wave and a particle

For a long time, scientists argued about whether light was a wave (like a ripple on water) or a stream of tiny particles (like a spray of bullets). The astonishing answer — discovered in the early 20th century — is that light is both, depending on how you look at it.

When light travels through space, it behaves like a wave: it spreads out, bends around corners, and can interfere with other light (causing patterns of bright and dark bands). But when light interacts with matter — when it is absorbed or emitted — it behaves like a particle: it arrives in one concentrated lump, not spread out like a wave.

That particle is the photon.

This idea — that light has both a wave nature and a particle nature simultaneously — is called wave-particle duality, and it is one of the foundational discoveries of quantum mechanics (the physics of the very small).
A photon has no mass, yet it is very real

A photon is completely massless. It weighs nothing at all — not even a trillionth of a trillionth of a gram. Yet it is absolutely real: it carries energy, and it carries momentum (the ability to push things). Sunlight physically pushes on surfaces it strikes. Solar sails — proposed spacecraft propulsion systems — work by riding this push from photons. Something with no mass is pushing a spacecraft through space. That is one of the genuinely strange features of reality.

How can something carry energy and momentum with no mass? Einstein's special relativity explains this: mass is not required to carry energy. For particles with zero mass, energy comes entirely from movement — and a photon always moves.
Photons always travel at the speed of light

Because a photon has zero mass, it travels at the fastest speed anything can travel in the universe: approximately 300,000 kilometres per second in a vacuum. This is called the speed of light, written as c. A photon has no choice in the matter — it must travel at exactly this speed. It cannot slow down or speed up.

When light travels through a medium like glass or water, photons interact with the atoms of that medium as they pass through, which effectively slows the light down. But in empty space, photons always travel at c, without exception.

Nothing with mass can ever reach the speed of light. Photons can reach it precisely because they have no mass.
What gives a photon its energy: frequency

Though all photons travel at the same speed, they do not all carry the same energy. The energy of a photon depends on its frequency — how rapidly it oscillates as a wave.

Picture an ocean wave: a wave that goes up and down fifty times per second has a higher frequency than one that goes up and down five times per second. Similarly, a photon can oscillate very slowly (low frequency) or very rapidly (high frequency).

The rule is simple: higher frequency = more energy per photon.

This relationship was first expressed by physicist Max Planck as the equation E = hf, where E is energy, h is a tiny constant (Planck's constant), and f is frequency. You do not need to memorize this, but the principle is important.

This is why X-ray photons can damage biological tissue — they have an extremely high frequency and therefore carry enormous energy per photon. Visible-light photons carry far less energy per photon, which is why sitting in sunlight (visible light) does not immediately injure you, but X-ray exposure must be carefully limited.
The electromagnetic spectrum: photons of all types

The word "photon" does not refer only to visible light. It refers to all electromagnetic radiation — a vast family of waves that differ only in their frequency. From lowest frequency to highest, this family is:

Radio waves → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma rays

All of these are made of photons. What differs between them is solely the frequency (and therefore energy) of those photons.

  • Radio wave photons: extremely low frequency, almost negligibly low energy. Your phone, Wi-Fi router, and radio station all communicate using photons of this type.
  • Microwave photons: slightly higher frequency. A microwave oven bombards food with these photons; water molecules absorb them and vibrate, producing heat.
  • Infrared photons: the "heat radiation" you feel when you hold your hand near a warm stove without touching it. Every warm object emits infrared photons.
  • Visible light photons: the narrow band of frequencies that your eyes can detect. Different colours correspond to slightly different frequencies — red is at the lower end, violet at the higher end.
  • Ultraviolet (UV) photons: just above visible light in frequency. These cause tanning and sunburn because they carry enough energy to damage skin cells.
  • X-ray photons: high frequency, high energy. They can pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by denser material like bone, which is why they produce skeletal images.
  • Gamma-ray photons: the highest frequency, highest energy photons in existence. Produced by nuclear reactions and radioactive decay. They can penetrate most materials and cause serious biological damage.

When scientists or engineers use the word "photon" without qualification, they often mean a visible-light photon, but the term correctly applies to the entire range above.
How photons are created

Photons are produced whenever a charged particle — most commonly an electron — loses energy.

Here is the most important mechanism: inside an atom, electrons occupy specific energy levels, like rungs on a ladder. An electron can absorb energy (from heat, from electricity, from a collision) and jump to a higher rung — an "excited" state. This is unstable. The electron quickly falls back down to a lower rung, and the energy it releases in doing so is emitted as a photon. The frequency of that photon is determined precisely by the size of the energy drop — a large drop produces a high-frequency (high-energy) photon, a small drop produces a low-frequency photon.

This is how:

  • The Sun shines — nuclear fusion drives electrons to excited states; they emit photons as they fall back.
  • Light bulbs work — electricity heats a tungsten filament; the hot atoms emit photons across a range of frequencies.
  • Neon signs glow — electricity excites neon gas atoms; they emit photons at very specific frequencies (giving neon its characteristic red-orange colour).
  • Lasers operate — they produce photons all at exactly the same frequency and in perfect synchrony, creating coherent, focused beams.
  • LEDs (light-emitting diodes) emit light — electrons drop across an energy gap in a semiconductor material and release photons.

Photons are also produced by:

  • Thermal radiation: any object with heat emits photons. The hotter it is, the higher the average frequency of emitted photons. A glowing red-hot coal emits visible-light photons; your body at 37°C emits infrared photons constantly (which is how thermal cameras can detect people in the dark).
  • Nuclear reactions: radioactive materials and nuclear explosions produce gamma-ray photons.
  • Matter-antimatter annihilation: when a particle of matter meets its antimatter twin, they destroy each other and the energy is converted entirely into photons.
How photons interact with matter

When a photon encounters matter, one of three things happens:

1. Absorption
The photon is absorbed by an atom or molecule. The atom gains the photon's energy — usually this shows up as heat or as an electron jumping to a higher energy level. Dark-coloured surfaces get hot in sunlight because they absorb most photons that hit them.

2. Reflection
The photon bounces off the surface. This is why you can see objects — the photons from a light source (the Sun, a lamp) hit objects around you and bounce toward your eyes. Colour is determined by which photons are reflected and which are absorbed: a red apple absorbs photons of most frequencies but reflects photons in the red-frequency range, which reach your eyes and cause you to perceive "red."

3. Transmission
The photon passes through the material without being absorbed or reflected. Glass and water transmit visible-light photons (which is why they are transparent). A window lets visible-light photons through but blocks many UV photons (which is why you cannot get a tan through most glass).

A crucial point: a photon is always absorbed or reflected as one complete, whole unit. It cannot be split in half or partially absorbed. This "all or nothing" quality is what it means to call it a quantum — a discrete, indivisible chunk. This was a radical departure from older physics, which assumed energy could flow in any smooth, continuous amount.
How you see: photons entering your eyes

Vision is photon detection.

Photons of visible light enter your eyes and land on your retina. There, specialized cells (rods and cones) contain molecules called photopigments. When a single photon is absorbed by one of these molecules, it triggers a chemical reaction that sends an electrical signal through the optic nerve to your brain. Your brain processes billions of these individual photon-detection events every second and assembles them into a continuous visual experience of the world.

The colours you see correspond to photon frequencies: photons of about 430 terahertz (trillion cycles per second) register as red; photons of about 750 terahertz register as violet. Everything in between — orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo — is a different frequency range.

In very dim conditions, your eyes can actually detect a single photon. The human eye is, in this sense, a remarkably sensitive photon detector.
Photons and the electromagnetic force

In modern physics, the photon has a role that goes deeper than simply being "light." It is the carrier of the electromagnetic force — one of nature's four fundamental forces.

When two electrically charged particles (such as two electrons) repel each other, how does the repulsion happen? They are not touching. Physics explains this by saying they exchange virtual photons — photons that cannot be directly observed, that exist only fleetingly as quantum messengers, transmitting the electromagnetic force between the particles. Every electric and magnetic interaction in the universe, from a compass needle aligning with Earth's magnetic field to the chemical bonds holding your body together, is mediated at the quantum level by photons. In this sense, the photon is not just light — it is the fundamental agent of one of the most important forces in nature.
Why the photon was a revolutionary discovery

Before the early 20th century, physicists assumed that light was a pure continuous wave, and that energy could be transferred in any arbitrary amount — a smooth flow. There was no reason to think of it as coming in chunks.

In 1905, Albert Einstein analysed an experiment called the photoelectric effect (where shining light on a metal causes it to emit electrons). The strange observation was that the intensity of the light did not matter for whether electrons were emitted — only the frequency did. Dim light of the right frequency ejected electrons; extremely bright light of too low a frequency ejected none at all.

Einstein explained this by proposing that light energy comes in discrete packets — what we now call photons — and that only a photon with sufficient frequency (sufficient energy per packet) could knock out an electron. No matter how much low-energy light you throw at the metal, no individual photon has enough energy to free an electron.

This was the birth of quantum mechanics, and it earned Einstein the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921. It shattered the assumption that nature is fundamentally smooth and continuous. At the smallest scales, energy is quantized — it comes in chunks, not smooth flows. The photon is the most vivid example of this.
Photons and time

Here is one of the most genuinely strange facts about photons: from a photon's own perspective, no time passes at all between the moment it is emitted and the moment it is absorbed.

Einstein's special relativity tells us that time slows down for objects moving faster — and at the exact speed of light, time stops entirely. A photon that takes 8 minutes (in our experience on Earth) to travel from the Sun to your eye experiences that journey as instantaneous. It has no duration of existence from its own frame of reference. It is created and destroyed in the same "moment," with no subjective passage of time, even if that journey spans billions of light-years.
Photons in the modern world

Almost all modern technology either uses photons or fundamentally relies on the understanding of them:

  • Solar cells (photovoltaic panels) convert photon energy directly into electricity via the photoelectric effect Einstein described.
  • Fibre-optic cables transmit internet data, phone calls, and video streams as pulses of photons through glass fibres at the speed of light.
  • Lasers are used in surgery, manufacturing, barcode scanners, DVD players, and optical communications.
  • Digital cameras and smartphones use sensor arrays to detect individual photons and convert them into pixel data.
  • Medical imaging: X-ray imaging uses high-energy photons; PET (positron emission tomography) scans detect gamma-ray photons from radioactive tracers in the body.
  • Remote controls communicate via infrared photons.
  • Quantum cryptography uses individual photons to transmit information in a way that is physically impossible to intercept without detection.
  • Photocopiers and laser printers use photons to imprint images onto charged drums.
Summary

A photon is the fundamental quantum (discrete packet) of electromagnetic energy. It is a massless particle that travels at the speed of light, carries energy proportional to its frequency, and forms the basis of all electromagnetic radiation — from radio waves to gamma rays. It behaves as both a wave and a particle. It is produced when electrons lose energy and drop to lower energy levels. When it encounters matter, it is either absorbed, reflected, or transmitted as a whole unit. It is the carrier of the electromagnetic force, the basis of all human vision, and the most consequential discovery of early quantum physics — the proof that nature, at its smallest scale, is fundamentally granular rather than smooth.
